segments.text: Hey friends, when a tired Vikram once again reached
home late from the office at 11:00 p.m., it had become a routine.
But today, something was different.
As he went to lie down near the bed,
he noticed a note placed on the drawer beside it.
Now, the note looked familiar.
But when Vikram read what was written inside, his heart
was completely shattered.
Tears began to roll down his eyes.
Written on the note were the words: “Worst Dad Ever.” Vikram had never expected
this, because until a few years ago, his eight-year-old daughter
used to make such notes every day and leave them in her dad’s drawer.
They would always say, “I love you, best dad ever.” But she had stopped
doing this for the past few years—and today, she had written this instead.
But why did this happen?
Hey friends, my name is Zeeshan and you’re watching Seeken, where we learn lessons
from books in a story format, in a simple and easy way.
If you want to achieve your goals in 2026, then the story I’m
about to share today is going to be very important for you.
Because here, you won’t just learn how to set goals.
Through this story, you’ll learn how to build systems that can help you improve
your health, relationships, money, and happiness.
Today, I’m going to share three powerful principles that can help you achieve
all your 2026 goals—and how you
can complete all three of these principles with just one practical action.
I’ll also explain how I can help you take that practical step.
At a very minimal cost—but you’ll learn about that at the end of the video.
Stay till the end—there’s a free gift for you as well.
Now, let’s go back to the story.
Thirty-three-year-old Vikram was the owner of a startup.
He had built his business through sheer hard work.
More than 20 employees worked for him, and his turnover was ₹2 crore.
From the outside, all of this made him look—and feel—quite successful.
But deep inside, he was slowly sinking into a swamp.
From 9:00 in the morning, he often had to work till 10 or 11:00 at night.
Constant decision-making and pressure
from all sides were taking a toll on his health.
He had become 30 kilos overweight.
Every New Year, he would donate money to a gym—but never really go.
That is, he would take a gym membership, but never actually go.
His blood pressure and sugar levels had both reached borderline levels.
He had many goals and many dreams.
He wanted to learn AI.
He wanted to go on a
world trip with his family—and he had promised this many times to his
loved ones.
But the truth was, he didn’t even have ten minutes to sit peacefully with his wife.
He was completely stuck in work—and things reached a breaking point
when his eight-year-old daughter’s birthday arrived.
This time, Vikram had promised from
the bottom of his heart that he would reach the party by 8:00 p.m.
But at 7:00 p.m., an urgent meeting call came in.
It was from his biggest client—one
he simply couldn’t afford to lose—and it was supposed to take just one hour.
The discussion dragged on and turned into three hours.
It was already 10:00 p.m.
There were 29 missed calls and more than 100 unread messages on his phone.
Even if he wanted to, he couldn’t bring himself to open them.
Somehow, when
he finally reached home at 11:00 p.m., the birthday party was already over.
His daughter had gone to her room crying and had fallen asleep.
Pieces of cake were lying on the dining table, and his wife was standing in front
of him. She wasn’t angry—there was just exhaustion on her face.
In fact, she said, “Vikram, I’m tired.
I’m tired of waiting—with our daughter—for you.
You make so many promises.
You set so many goals and fill our hearts with hope that things will get
better from now on.” But in reality, none of that is actually happening.
And after this, when he went near his bed, he saw that note—the moment he saw it,
tears rolled down his eyes.
He was extremely sleepy, but his sleep vanished.
With tears
in his eyes, he decided that no matter what, he would have to change his life.
At the same time, while he was checking his messages, he saw
a text from his friend Isaac.
Now, Isaac was an old friend from the same IIM batch and owned a very large
company of his own—a manufacturing business.
His company was much bigger
than Vikram’s, with more than 200 employees working for him.
Yet, somehow, despite all this, he still managed to go to the gym every morning.
He used to drop his child to school, went on regular vacations with
his family, and kept learning new courses.
Vikram knew all of this.
And to be honest, it often irritated him—how could Isaac manage to do so much?
Many times, Vikram would tell himself that Isaac was just very lucky.
But today, putting his ego aside, he replied to him and said, “I need
to meet you.” The next day, Vikram and Isaac met at a coffee shop.
After meeting
him, when Isaac looked at Vikram, he could see that he was in bad shape.
There were dark circles under his eyes, his health looked terrible.
Seeing all this, he asked Vikram, “What’s going on?” Usually, Vikram would always
say, “Everything is fine.”
But today, he opened up completely and poured his heart out.
One by one, he told him everything—how there
was immense pressure in his business, how he had no time to work on his
health, and in fact, how he couldn’t even attend his own child’s birthday.
All of this had completely worn him down.
Then Isaac said to him, “It’s okay. A new year is coming.
Have you set any goals for this new year?”
Then Vikram said, “Every year I do it, yaar—I set goals to go to the
gym, follow a diet, travel, learn a new course, and grow my business.
But none of those goals ever get completed.
I don’t know why.
Maybe I’m setting the wrong goals,
or maybe I just don’t have discipline.” Isaac stopped him and said, “No.
You do have discipline—and you do have goals.” “You are setting them correctly.
That’s not the problem.
What you need is one thing—what we call systematic thinking.
You’ve done an MBA, you’ve built a business.
That means you do have discipline.
You can set goals.
But goals
don’t get completed until there’s a thinking process behind them—a system.
A process-driven life, where you can get things done even without relying solely
on willpower or motivation.” After hearing this, Vikram asked, “Yes, I’ve heard all
this, but
how do I actually do it?” Well, Isaac said, “Theoretically, it’s very simple.
But to do it practically, you’ll need my help.
The truth is, a few years ago, I was in the same situation as you.
I used to work on my business all day, from morning till night.”
My health wasn’t good back then.
Today, I go to the gym, spend time with my children, keep
learning new courses, and in fact, I’m even pursuing a new degree.
I also travel regularly—and all of this is happening because I use three powerful
principles from three powerful books,
and I complete each of these principles by taking one action every week.
Vikram asked him, “Please, please tell me—how do I build a
system too?” Then he started explaining the three principles one by one.
Principle No. 1: Holistic vs Partial Thinking.
Isaac said that whenever a
person sets a goal, they usually do it with partial thinking.
For example, if someone’s goal
is fitness, they set it as if fitness is the only thing in their life.
And as long as they are thinking partially, focusing only on fitness…
He thinks, “Yes, I’ll wake up in the morning, I’ll drink water, I’ll even
hire a trainer.” Everything seems possible to him—but none of it actually happens.
Why? Because
he isn’t thinking holistically, and the same thing is happening with you too.
Vikram asked, “So what does that mean?
Should I think negatively? “No,” Isaac replied.
Realistically, Isaac asks, “Tell me, what fitness goals did
you actually set?” Vikram thinks and replies about last year, “I had thought
that I would lose weight and for that, I would go to the gym.
I planned to go
to the gym after I’m free from the office, take my time, work out there from 7
to 8 or 9, eat my meals, spend time with my family, and then go to sleep.”
“This was the plan I made last year to achieve my goal,” he said.
Then Isaac asked, “So why did this plan fail?” Vikram replied, “Because, yaar!
Many times, my office didn’t finish by 7:00 p.m.
Sometimes it would go till 8, sometimes longer.
There would be traffic, client calls would come in.
And even if I managed to reach, I would be so tired that I didn’t feel
like going to the gym at all.” Isaac said, “Exactly, see—that’s the problem.
When we think about a goal and write it down, we only think positively.
Only one thing comes to our mind, but we don’t consider all
the negative factors around it that could happen.
That’s why Principle Number One is to understand things holistically.”
Start thinking.
Start thinking
that yes, there’s fitness, but along with that, you also have to handle fatigue.
Client calls might come.
There could be fights at home. Many things could happen.
You need to understand all of this and set your goals holistically.
Then, moving on to Principle Number Two: Worst-Day Planning.
See, the second mistake most people make is that whenever they set a goal,
they plan it based on their best day—thinking, “I’ll wake up at this time
in the morning, then I’ll do this, then that.” Then, “I’ll go to the gym.
After that, I’ll read a book. Then, I’ll do office work.
I’ll do this task, that task,”—and so on.
They plan their day based on their best day.
But it should be exactly the opposite.
You need to make a worst-day plan.
That means, imagine your goal—you have to go to the gym.
The “best day”
scenario is when nothing interrupts you—no client calls, no disturbances.
When there’s no function, no fight with your wife, no important work
with the kids, and everyone is healthy—that’s the best day.
The worst day is when all these things could happen.
Then what will you do?
Will your 7:00 a.m. plan still work?
Vikram said, “No, exactly—it won’t work like that.
So what should I do?” Then Isaac said, “Reduce friction as much as possible.
In the beginning, going to the gym involves many steps.
To go to the gym at 7:00 a.m., there shouldn’t be any client calls, no traffic,
no fatigue.
That means you’ll need a lot of willpower and motivation just to go to the gym.
So instead, think of something you
can do even on your worst day.” Even if client calls come, you can still do it.
Even if there’s a fight with your wife, you can still do it.
Even if you get stuck in traffic, you can still do it.
Then, both of them thought for two or three minutes,
and that’s when Isaac gave an idea:
if the goal is to work on fitness, why not do 10–15 exercises at the office itself?
You can do that.
Vikram said, “Yaar, that’s a solid idea.
Because this will remove all the friction.
Even if there’s traffic, it’s no problem.
I can rest directly when I get home.
Even if there’s a fight, it’s okay. I can work alone at the office.
No matter what happens, I can
at least spare 10 minutes—to do push-ups, to do dips.” Isaac
said, “Yes.” “Yes, obviously, you probably won’t get a six-pack from this.
But your health journey will start. Just remember one thing.
To understand this principle, keep this
in mind: plan for the worst day, not for the best day.
And the last, third principle—Band-Aid Removal—is this: see, the fitness goal
you just set, the plan you made, has become like putting a
Band-Aid on the problem.” Obviously, this won’t give you six-pack abs.
The third principle is that instead of short-term fixes—like
putting a Band-Aid—you need to focus on the root cause.
That means, whatever problems come
in your way to going to the gym, you should find ways to avoid them.
Doing exercises at the office
is fine, but you should create a system, develop habits for yourself, so that all
these problems are permanently solved—and you still get time to go to the gym.
For example, you start going to the gym at 6:00 a.m.
In the morning, your willpower will be full, and no one will disturb you.
Just prepare your clothes the night before so you’re ready in the morning.
Yes, waking up at 6:00 a.m.
will be difficult, but it can be done.
If you start going to bed early and have dinner early, you’ll
notice how it becomes easier.
Everything is connected, but
once this system is in place, your health goal will be achieved.
In the same way, you can do this for your business too.
For example, in business, you have to work two to three hours every day.
You’re doing deep work, starting Pomodoro sessions, and
handling a lot of tasks—but why not take a step back and create
a system so that you don’t even have to spend those two hours on that work?
Have someone else do that work on your behalf.
Basically, for Principle No.
Three, just remember one thing: you need
a systematic approach, not a Band-Aid approach or a quick-fix hack.
This will create a long-term solution.
After this, Isaac explained that, “See, all three things are simple
in theory, but applying them practically is the most important part.
And to apply them practically, you don’t need much—just one thing.” Vikram asked,
“What is that one thing?” Well, that one thing is what I
started doing—weekly meetings.
You can take it as a challenge and hold a weekly review meeting
with yourself every week.
Set your goals—whether small or big—and spend one hour meeting with yourself.
In the beginning, if you want, I can help you.
In this meeting, basically, what we’ll do is: we’ll set a goal
for the week, and then after a week, we’ll review it.
We’ll check all three
principles—was the goal we set based on partial thinking or holistic thinking?
Because many times, after setting a goal, we realize, “Yes, this problem could also
come up.” You might even face problems doing 10–15 minutes of gym at the office.
For example, if you’re not sure what exercises to do, the
solution for that can be discussed in this meeting.
Any negative
points that you haven’t understood yet will be reviewed in this meeting.
Then, using Principle Number
One and Principle Number Two, we’ll create a plan that also addresses those
problems, and with Principle Three, we’ll again focus weekly on building a system.
If we dedicate half an hour to an hour each week
to these three things, we’ll understand them better and get a strong start.
Isaac explained, “Vikram, I focused on this one thing for six months to a year.
I held weekly meetings, set goals for myself—asking, ‘Why did it happen?
Why didn’t it happen?’ I worked on that.
And today, I’ve created a system for myself where I have time for health,
time for my family, time for travel, and I’m earning much more money than
before.” After hearing all this, Vikram said, “Look, I think
your system is very powerful, but obviously I can’t do it alone.
So here’s what we do—let’s start attending weekly meetings together.
I’ll spend half an hour with myself, and you help me for
half an hour.” Now, Isaac happily agreed to this.
Then Vikram and Isaac started holding this meeting every Sunday.
In these meetings, Isaac would set goals with Vikram.
Vikram would try to achieve those goals over the week.
Sometimes he would succeed, sometimes he wouldn’t.
Whenever he didn’t, they would analyze it in the weekly meeting, plan holistically,
consider the worst-case scenarios, and start creating a system together.
Gradually, Vikram began to see results.
Now he started going
to bed early, which allowed him to wake up early in the morning and go to the gym.
After that, he would go to the office in a positive mood, which meant fewer
arguments at home.
He had created a system such that at 6:00 a.m., no matter what happens—whether
there’s a client call or not—he would leave home and go to the gym.
After that, for his health, he started going for a walk at night after dinner.
His relationship with his wife and child improved.
He continued this for a few
months, and as a result, his relationship with his wife got much better.
His health started improving.
In his business, where people used to take him lightly before, now seeing
his seriousness, everyone’s output improved.
His income started increasing, and guess what—it took six months, but after
six months, he saw a note again near his bed, which read: “Best Dad Ever.
I love you.” Just from one keystone habit, Vikram had changed his entire life.
Just like uploading a video every Sunday is my keystone habit that
changed my life, I feel the same about one keystone habit for him.
If you also start doing weekly meetings with me, this can completely change
your entire life.
If you want me to hold weekly meetings with you in 2026, we can have a

So in 2026, you can achieve even your biggest goals,
